William Henry Harrison's inauguration. On March 4, 1841, Harrison delivered what would become the longest presidential inaugural address in American history, a speech that stretched nearly two hours. The moment proved to be his most lasting legacy. Harrison was 68 years old at the time, the oldest president to take office until then, and he delivered his lengthy address in cold, wet conditions without adequate winter clothing. Disaster followed swiftly. Just 31 days into his presidency, on April 4, 1841, Harrison died of pneumonia or related complications, becoming the shortest presidency in United States history. His inaugural address championed manifest destiny and westward expansion while emphasizing limits on executive power and the supremacy of Congress, directly opposing the expansion of presidential authority under Andrew Jackson. One historical consequence emerged from this tragedy: his vice president, John Tyler, became the first to assume the presidency mid-term, establishing a succession precedent that would shape American constitutional practice for centuries to come.
